Final post in this 5-part series. Parts 1-4 built one agent per pipeline stage:
preprocessing (tool use), training (planning), postprocessing (reflection), and error
analysis (evaluation). This post wires all four together as a multi-agent system --
and, deliberately, puts the error-analysis agent at the center of the design rather
than treating it as the last step in a line.
:::

## The core idea: multi-agent communication patterns

A multi-agent system is just: several agents, each with its own role-appropriate
tools, talking to each other in some pattern. The course lays out four patterns, in
roughly increasing order of power and decreasing order of predictability:

1. **Linear pipeline** -- agent A's output feeds agent B, feeds agent C. Simplest,
   most common, easiest to debug.
2. **Hierarchical / manager-coordinated** -- a manager agent dispatches to team
   members and collects results back through itself (not agent-to-agent directly --
   routing everything through the manager keeps the wiring tractable).
3. **Deep hierarchy** -- sub-agents that themselves have sub-agents. More powerful
   decomposition, meaningfully harder to reason about.
4. **All-to-all** -- every agent can message every other agent whenever it wants.
   Most expressive, least predictable; the course is explicit that this suits
   applications with a real tolerance for chaos, not production pipelines.

## Why a straight linear pipeline is the wrong shape here

If you mechanically chain Parts 1-4 -- preprocess, then train, then postprocess, then
analyze errors -- you get a linear pipeline. It's tempting, and it's what most tutorials
would show you. But think about what actually happens when error analysis finds that
**the model is the dominant root cause**: in a strict linear pipeline, that insight has
nowhere to go. It's the last stage. The pipeline finishes, a human reads a report, and
maybe next month someone remembers to retrain.

That's the exact failure this series exists to prevent. If error analysis is the
highest-ROI agentic workflow (Part 4's whole argument), it can't be a dead-end report --
it needs to be able to **route work back** to the training and postprocessing agents.
That's a hierarchical pattern, not a linear one, and the manager in that hierarchy is
the error-analysis agent itself.

## The design: error-analysis-as-manager

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    EA[Error-Analysis Agent<br/>manager] -->|dispatches| PRE[Preprocessing Agent]
    EA -->|dispatches| TRAIN[Training Agent]
    EA -->|dispatches| POST[Postprocessing Agent]
    PRE -->|trace + notes| EA
    TRAIN -->|new model checkpoint| EA
    POST -->|cleaned masks| EA
    EA -->|weekly tally + routed fix| HUMAN[Human review]
```

Concretely: the error-analysis agent runs on a schedule (a cron job, in my own setup),
pulls a batch of recent predictions, tallies root causes the way Part 4 built, and then
-- instead of just writing a report -- **calls the agent responsible for the dominant
component** with a targeted instruction.

```python
from openai import OpenAI
import json

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1", api_key="local")
MODEL = "Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B"

# --- the three "team member" agents from Parts 1-3, exposed as callable tools ------

def preprocessing_agent(instruction: str) -> str:
    """Runs the Part 1 tool-use agent (normalize_xray, tile_image, check_saturation)
    with a specific instruction, e.g. 'tighten the saturation threshold to 0.5%'."""
    ...  # calls run_agent(instruction) from Part 1

def training_agent(instruction: str) -> str:
    """Runs the Part 2 planning agent, e.g. 'retrain the void head with a higher
    Focal Tversky recall weight, val split stratified by defect class'."""
    ...  # calls plan_training_run(instruction) from Part 2, then executes the plan

def postprocessing_agent(instruction: str) -> str:
    """Runs the Part 3 reflection agent, e.g. 'lower min_blob_area, containment rule
    violations are showing up on the new lot'."""
    ...  # calls generate_postprocessing_config + reflect_and_fix from Part 3

TEAM = {
    "PREPROCESSING": preprocessing_agent,
    "MODEL": training_agent,
    "POSTPROCESSING": postprocessing_agent,
}

# --- the Part 4 error-analysis agent, now acting as manager -----------------------

def run_weekly_error_analysis_cycle(traces: list) -> dict:
    tally = build_error_tally(traces)              # from Part 4
    dominant = max(tally, key=tally.get)
    if tally[dominant] < 5:
        return {"status": "no dominant failure mode this week", "tally": tally}

    # Ask the manager LLM to turn the tally + notes into a concrete instruction for
    # whichever team member agent owns the dominant component.
    notes = [t.component_notes.get("root_cause", "") for t in traces
             if dominant in t.component_notes.get("root_cause", "").upper()]
    resp = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=MODEL,
        messages=[{"role": "system", "content":
                   f"You manage a segmentation pipeline team. This week's dominant "
                   f"failure mode is {dominant} ({tally[dominant]} of "
                   f"{sum(tally.values())} failures). Write ONE specific, actionable "
                   f"instruction for the {dominant} agent, grounded in these notes."},
                  {"role": "user", "content": "\n".join(notes[:10])}],
    )
    instruction = resp.choices[0].message.content
    result = TEAM[dominant](instruction)
    return {"status": "routed", "tally": tally, "dominant": dominant,
            "instruction": instruction, "result": result}
```

Note what this buys you over a linear pipeline: the manager routes to **exactly one**
team member -- whichever the tally says is the actual bottleneck -- instead of
mechanically re-running the whole chain. That's the frequency x fixability
prioritization from Part 4, now automated instead of just reported.

## Where hierarchy is enough, and where it isn't

I'd stop at one level of hierarchy for this use case, and I'd say so explicitly rather
than let the series imply "more agent-to-agent freedom is always better." A deep
hierarchy (e.g. the training agent having its own sub-agents for hyperparameter search
and data augmentation) or an all-to-all pattern (every agent free to message every
other agent about anything) would both genuinely reduce your ability to predict what
the pipeline does on a given week -- and for something that touches real training
compute and real production masks, that unpredictability is a cost, not a feature. The
course's own caveat applies directly: all-to-all suits applications you're willing to
re-run and shrug off if the output isn't great. A defect-detection pipeline in a
semiconductor fab is not that application.

## Copilot / MCP angle, end to end

Every one of the four agents in this post is already an MCP tool by the end of Part 4
(`preprocessing-tools`, plus equivalent servers for training, postprocessing, and error
analysis). Registering all of them means you can drive the entire hierarchy from a
single Copilot chat session: *"run this week's error analysis and fix whatever's
dominant"* -- Copilot's own agent-mode planning becomes the manager, calling your four
MCP servers in whatever order it decides. The hand-written `run_weekly_error_analysis_cycle`
above is the version I'd actually trust unattended on a cron job, precisely because its
routing logic is explicit and reviewable, not delegated to another agent's internal
planning. Use Copilot's version for interactive exploration; use the explicit version
for anything that runs while you're not watching.

## Which model to use

The manager role (turning a tally into one specific instruction) is a genuinely
harder judgment task than any single component agent, since it has to weigh evidence
and commit to a prioritization. This is where I'd spend a better model's budget if
you're going to spend it anywhere in this series -- a frontier API model for the
manager step, and your free/local model (Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, or a free OpenRouter
tier model if you don't have local hardware) for the four worker agents, which are
each doing a narrower, better-specified job.

## Closing this series

Five posts, one course, one pipeline: tool use turned preprocessing into something you
can drive by request instead of by script; planning let a training run adapt its steps
to what was actually asked; reflection gave postprocessing a cheap self-correction
loop grounded in real domain rules instead of vibes; and error analysis -- deliberately
the centerpiece -- became the manager that decides where the other three should spend
their effort next. None of this replaces the underlying segmentation science (loss
functions, domain rules like p2/p98 normalization or void-appears-bright physics still
have to be right); what it replaces is the manual, easy-to-skip work of *deciding
what to fix next*, which is exactly the step most teams don't do consistently -- and
exactly why it was worth building an agent for.
